statement: Christine Nicholls, "What does Jukurrpa ('Dreamtime', 'the Dreaming') mean? A semantic and conceptual journey of discovery," Australian Aboriginal Studies (AIATSIS), 2014, documents Jukurrpa's five interrelated senses (ancestral era, ancestral beings, manifestations of their power, binding law, personal totemic inheritance) and argues the English gloss "Dreaming"/"Dreamtime" is historically entrenched but inadequate. W.E.H. Stanner's foundational essay "The Dreaming" (in Australian Signpost, ed. T.A.G. Hungerford, Melbourne: F.W. Cheshire, 1956, pp. 51-65 — not 1953/Traditional Aboriginal Society as sometimes cited) drew primarily on Stanner's own Murinbata (Daly River) fieldwork, not Yolŋu, Warlpiri, or any of the other specific traditions this gloss is now conventionally applied to. Later scholarship has directly critiqued the flattening effect of the umbrella term: Patrick Wolfe, "On Being Woken Up: The Dreamtime in Anthropology and in Australian Settler Culture," Comparative Studies in Society and History 33(2) (1991): 197-224; Maureen Perkins, "Timeless Cultures: The 'Dreamtime' as Colonial Discourse," Time & Society 7(2) (1998): 335-351, arguing the "timelessness" framing is itself a colonial-era construction. Distinct terms across the traditions researched in this batch: Yolŋu Wangarr, Warlpiri Jukurrpa, Pitjantjatjara/Yankunytjatjara Tjukurpa, Arrernte Altyerre.

does_not_demonstrate: That "the Dreaming" is a native pan-Aboriginal self-description rather than a later English gloss retrofitted from Stanner's Murinbata-based essay onto genuinely distinct traditions
